annotations.annotation_text: Page 16 opens Book 1, Chapter 1 ("The Fall of Finnegan") during the Age of Gods (Theocratic) phase. This passage continues the mythic fall of Tim Finnegan / HCE, the thunderclap awakening primitive religion, and the recumbent giant embedded in the Dublin landscape, featuring HCE, Finn MacCool, Mutt and Jute. The nocturnal dream-narrative layers Dublin topography, world mythology, and linguistic alchemy into polysemic prose.
sources: Campbell, Joseph and Robinson, Henry Morton. A Skeleton Key to Finnegans Wake. https://archive.org/details/skeletonkeytofin00camp
McHugh, Roland. Annotations to Finnegans Wake. https://archive.org/details/annotationstofin0000mchu_h5g8
Gordon, John. Finnegans Wake: A Plot Summary. https://johngordonfinnegan.weebly.com
JJDA: Finnegans Wake Genetic Edition. https://jjda.ie

annotations.annotation_text: Clontarf historical locus (016.02): the site of Brian Boru's climactic 1014 victory over the Norsemen. In Joyce's historiography, conqueror and native butcher one another only to decompose together and enrich the fertile Dublin soil.
sources: Curtis, Edmund. A History of Ireland. https://archive.org/details/historyofireland0000curt
O'Donovan, John. Annals of the Four Masters. https://celt.ucc.ie/published/T100005A/

annotations.annotation_text: Portmanteau "beseeking" (016.10): beseeching (prayer/petition) + besieging (military encirclement). The invading Norseman simultaneously begs for hospitality and threatens violent siege across the cultural divide.

Mid-page polysemic node on page 16 ("The Fall of Finnegan"): Joyce weaves multilingual puns across 60+ languages — etymological roots from the Contemporary Literature Press lexicons (Romanian, Scandinavian, Slavic, Classical) intersect with local Dublin speech rhythms. The Age of Gods (Theocratic) dream-logic transforms ordinary syntax into a palimpsest of global literary and mythic references.
sources: Tindall, William York. A Reader's Guide to Finnegans Wake. https://archive.org/details/readersguidetofi00tind
Contemporary Literature Press: Multilingual Lexicons for FW. https://editura.mttlc.ro
Atherton, James S. The Books at the Wake. https://archive.org/details/booksatwake0000athe

annotations.annotation_text: Excavation motif (016.18): the dialogue uncovers subsurface strata of Dublin—Viking spearheads, Celtic torcs, Dutch clay pipes, and crushed skulls—demonstrating that history is a palimpsest of buried matter awaiting decipherment.
sources: Mink, Louis O. A Finnegans Wake Gazetteer. https://archive.org/details/finneganswakegaz0000mink
Joyce, P.W. The Origin and History of Irish Names of Places. https://archive.org/details/originandhistory01joycuoft

annotations.annotation_text: Tavern/jury motif "bar" on page 16 ("The Fall of Finnegan"): the twelve customers drinking in HCE's Chapelizod pub represent public opinion, the Zodiac, and the Apostles within the mythic fall of Tim Finnegan / HCE, the thunderclap awakening primitive religion, and the recumbent giant embedded in the Dublin landscape. During this Age of Gods (Theocratic) phase, they judge, condemn, and demand another round — the Greek chorus of middle-class Dublin gossip.
sources: Glasheen, Adaline. Third Census of Finnegans Wake. https://archive.org/details/thirdcensusoffin0000glas
Campbell, Joseph and Robinson, Henry Morton. A Skeleton Key. https://archive.org/details/skeletonkeytofin00camp
Gordon, John. Finnegans Blog (Tavern chapters). https://johngordonfinnegan.weebly.com

annotations.annotation_text: Germanic greeting "gutenmorg" (016.25): German 'Guten Morgen' / Danish 'god morgen'. The foreign invader attempts civil communication, marking the linguistic influx of Germanic tongues into Gaelic Ireland.
sources: Contemporary Literature Press: German in FW. https://editura.mttlc.ro
